input: Before Einstein came up with his special theory of relativity, people had already noticed that particles moving very fast seem to gain mass. And the correct formula for this had already been found. In fcat, Lorentz had already worked out the formulas known as the "Lorentz transformation," which contain the full mathematical core of the special theory of relativity. But it was Einstein who demonstrated that all of this was what we should have expected, and not just a set of temporary fixes to epxlain surprising experimental results. Still, we should not fogret that experimental results were the original reason for the whole theroy. And they have remained the basis for the huge logical rebuilding that Einstein's theories involve. We can now sum up the reasons why it became necessary to replace space and time with "space-time." The old way of separating space and time was based on the belief that there was no problem in saying that two events in faraway places happened at the same time. So people thought we could describe the layout of the universe at a given moment using only spatial terms. But now that simultaneity depends on a particular observer, this is no longer possible. What one observer describes as the state of the world at a given moment, another observer sees as a series of events at different times. And the relations between them are not just spatial but also temporal. For the same reason, we deal with events rather than with bodies. In the old theory, it was possible to think about a number of bodies all at the same moment. And snice the time was the same for all of them, it could be ignored. But now we cannot do that if we want an objective account of physical occurrences. We must state the date at which a body is to be considered. And so we arrive at an "event," meaning something that happesn at a given time. When we know the time and place of an event in one observer's system of reckoning, we can work out its time and place according to another observer. But we must know the time as well as the place, because we can no longer ask what its plaec is for the new observer at the "saem" time as for the old observer. There is no such thing as the "same" time for different observers, unless they are at rest relative to each other.
output: The apparent increase of mass in swiftly moving particles had been observed, and the right formula had been found, before Einstein invented his special theory of relativity. In fact, Lorentz had arrived at the formulæ called the “Lorentz transformation,” which embody the whole mathematical essence of the special theory of relativity. But it was Einstein who showed that the whole thing was what we ought to have expected, and not a set of makeshift devices to account for surprising experimental results. Nevertheless, it must not be forgotten that experimental results were the original motive of the whole theory, and have remained the ground for undertaking the tremendous logical reconstruction involved in Einstein’s theories. We may now recapitulate the reasons which have made it necessary to substitute “space-time” for space and time. The old separation of space and time rested upon the belief that there was no ambiguity in saying that two events in distant places happened at the same time; consequently it was thought that we could describe the topography of the universe at a given instant in purely spatial terms. But now that simultaneity has become relative to a particular observer, this is no longer possible. What is, for one observer, a description of the state of the world at a given instant, is, for another observer, a series of events at various different times, whose relations are not merely spatial but also temporal. For the same reason, we are concerned with events, rather than with bodies. In the old theory, it was possible to consider a number of bodies all at the same instant, and since the time was the same for all of them it could be ignored. But now we cannot do that if we are to obtain an objective account of physical occurrences. We must mention the date at which a body is to be considered, and thus we arrive at an “event,” that is to say, something which happens at a given time. When we know the time and place of an event in one observer’s system of reckoning, we can calculate its time and place according to another observer. But we must know the time as well as the place, because we can no longer ask what is its place for the new observer at the “same” time as for the old observer. There is no such thing as the “same” time for different observers, unless they are at rest relatively to each other.

Then came the discovery of the electron, a small finite unit of negative electricity, and the proton, a small finite unit of positive electricity. Thus physics has had to digest new facts and face new problems. But the problems raised by the electron and the quantum are not those that the theory of relativity can solve, at any rate at present; as yet, it throws no light upon the discontinuities which exist in nature. The problems solved by the special theory of relativity are typified by the Michelson-Morley experiment. Assuming the correctness of Maxwell’s theory of electromagnetism, there should have been certain discoverable effects of motion through the ether; in fact, there were none. Then there was the observed fact that a body in very rapid motion appears to increase its mass; the increase is in the ratio of OP to MP in the figure in the preceding chapter. Facts of this sort gradually accumulated, until it became imperative to find some theory which would account for them all. Maxwell’s theory reduced itself to certain equations, known as “Maxwell’s equations.” Through all the revolutions which physics has undergone in the last fifty years, these equations have remained standing; indeed they have continually grown in importance as well as in certainty—for Maxwell’s arguments in their favor were so shaky that the correctness of his results must almost be ascribed to intuition. Now these equations were, of course, obtained from experiments in terrestrial laboratories, but there was a tacit assumption that the motion of the earth through the ether could be ignored.

output: Perhaps even this exception may not long remain. There are parts of physics which, so far, lie outside the general theory of relativity, but there are no parts of physics to which it is not in some degree relevant. And its importance to philosophy is perhaps even greater than its importance to physics. It has, of course, been seized upon by philosophers of different schools as affording support to their respective nostrums; St. Thomas, Kant, and Hegel are claimed to have anticipated it. But I do not think that any of the philosophers who make these suggestions have taken the trouble to understand the theory. For my part, I do not profess to know exactly what its philosophical consequences will prove to be, but I am convinced that they are far-reaching, and quite different from what they seem to philosophers who are ignorant of mathematics. The points of space-time have, of course, no duration as well as no spatial extension. It is generally assumed that several events may occupy the same point; this is involved in the conception of the intersection of world-lines. I think it may also be assumed that one event may extend over a finite extent of space-time, but on this point the theory is silent, so far as I know. I shall myself, in a later chapter, deal with the construction of points as systems of events, each of which events has a finite extension; this is a subject which has been especially treated by Dr Whitehead, but I shall suggest a method somewhat different from his. So long as we confine ourselves to the theory of relativity, it is not necessary to consider whether events have a finite extension, though I think it is necessary to assume that two events may both occupy the same point of space-time. Even on this, however, there is a certain vagueness in the authoritative expositions, which is due mainly to the large scale of the phenomena with which the theory is principally concerned. Sometimes it would seem as if the whole earth counted as a point; certainly one physical laboratory does so in the practice of writers on relativity. On occasion, Professor Eddington considers an area of square kilometres to be an infinitesimal of the second order. The fact that such a view is appropriate in discussions of relativity makes it unnecessary to be precise as to what is meant by saying that two events occupy the same point, or that two world-lines intersect.

On the question of a largest uint for events, the arguments are more about logic than about experience. In one sense, any series of events can be called a event. What I mean is that anything happening at the same time as everything that happened during the Battle of Waterloo is a mix of parts that are not all happening at the same time as each other. Whether we call a mix like this "event" or not is just a matter of words. But if our goal is to show the structure of the world, it is clear that we must tell apart objects that have structure from those that are only parts of such structures. So it is useful to have a word for the latter. The word I will use is "event." But I will not go so far as to say that an "event" must have no structure. I will only assume that whatever structure it may have does not matter for physics or for psychology. In other words, that its parts, if it has any, do not have relations to other objects that science can tell apart. When the word "event" is used in this sense, it is clear that, as far as our experience goes, no event lasts more than a few seconds at most. There is no reason before experience why this should be so. It is just a fact from experience. But I think a way of speaking that hides this can only cause confusion. For the reasons above, I cannot accept Dr Whitehead's building of points by means of enclosure-series as a answer to the problem it is meant to solve.

input: Science does not use the old "law of causality,". But it does use something we can call the "uniformity of nature,". Or rather it accepts this based on inductive reasons. The uniformity of nature does not claim the simple idea of "same cause, same effect." It claims that laws stay the same over time. That means if a law has held true in the past we can observe, for example, a law showing acceleration as a function of the setup, we expect it to keep holding in future. Or if that law itself does not hold, then some other law that matches the expected law for the past will hold for the future. The basis for this idea is just the inductive reason that it has been found true in very many cases. So this idea cannot be certain, only probable to a degree we cannot measure exactly. The uniformity of nature in this sense is used in scientific practice. But we should not treat it in its general form as a kind of main premise that all scientific reasoning needs to avoid bieng wrong. The assumpiton that all laws of nature are permanent has less probability than the assumption that one particular law is permanent. And the assumption that a particular law is permanent forever has less probability than the assumption that it will hold until a certain date. In any given case, science will assume what the case needs, but nothing more. Whne making the Nautical Almanac for 1915, it will assume the law of gravitation stays true until the end of that year. But it will not make any assumption about 1916 until the next volume of the amlanac comes. This way of doing things is driven by the fact that the uniformity of nature is not known a priori. It is an empirical genearlisation, like "all men are mortal." In all such cases, it is better to reason directly from the given particular cases to the new case than to reason through a main premise. The conclusion is only probable either way. But it gets a higher probability with the first method than with the second. In all science we have to tell aprat two kinds of laws: first, those that can be checked by experience but are probably only approximate. Second, those that cannot be checked but may be exact.
output: (4) Although the old "law of causality" is not assumed by science, something which we may call the "uniformity of nature" is assumed, or rather is accepted on inductive grounds. The uniformity of nature does not assert the trivial principle "same cause, same effect," but the principle of the permanence of laws. That is to say, when a law exhibiting, e.g. an acceleration as a function of the configuration has been found to hold throughout the observable past, it is expected that it will continue to hold in the future, or that, if it does not itself hold, there is some other law, agreeing with the supposed law as regards the past, which will hold for the future. The ground of this principle is simply the inductive ground that it has been found to be true in very many instances; hence the principle cannot be considered certain, but only probable to a degree which cannot be accurately estimated. The uniformity of nature, in the above sense, although it is assumed in the practice of science, must not, in its generality, be regarded as a kind of major premiss, without which all scientific reasoning would be in error. The assumption that all laws of nature are permanent has, of course, less probability than the assumption that this or that particular law is permanent; and the assumption that a particular law is permanent for all time has less probability than the assumption that it will be valid up to such and such a date. Science, in any given case, will assume what the case requires, but no more. In constructing the Nautical Almanac for 1915 it will assume that the law of gravitation will remain true up to the end of that year; but it will make no assumption as to 1916 until it comes to the next volume of the almanac. This procedure is, of course, dictated by the fact that the uniformity of nature is not known a priori, but is an empirical generalisation, like "all men are mortal." In all such cases, it is better to argue immediately from the given particular instances to the new instance, than to argue by way of a major premiss; the conclusion is only probable in either case, but acquires a higher probability by the former method than by the latter. In all science we have to distinguish two sorts of laws: first, those that are empirically verifiable but probably only approximate; secondly, those that are not verifiable, but may be exact.

But the argument does not change much based on which definition we pick. In general, a teleological system is one where purposes get fulfilled, meaning certain desires, the deeper, nobler, more basic, more universal ones. Or whatever kind, actually happen. The fact, if it is a fact, that the universe is mechanical has nothing to do with whether it is teleological in that sense. There could be a mechanical system where all wishes come true. And there could be one where all wishes are blocked. So whether our actual world is teleological. Or how much it is, cannot be decided by showing it is mechanical. And wanting it to be teleological is not a reason to wish it were not mechanical. In all these questions, it is very hard to avoid mixing up what we can infer wiht what is actually determined. Let us think for a moment about the different ways the future might be "determined." There is one sense, a very important one, in which it is determined completely apart from scientific laws, namely that it will be whatever it will be. We all treat the past as determined simply because it has already happened. If memory worked forward instead of backward, we would treat the future as equally determined because it will happen. "But," people tell us, "you cannot change the past, while you can change the future to some extent." This view, it seems to me, rests on exactly those mistakes about causation that I have been trying to clear away. You cannot make past different from what it was, true. But that is just an application of the law of contradiction. If you already know what the past was, it is obviously pointless to wish it were different. But you also cannot make the future different from what it will be. This too is an application of the law of contradiction. And if you happen to know the future, for example, a coming eclipse, it is just as pointless to wish it different as to wish the past different.

output: Our solution of this problem has to satisfy certain conditions. It has to bring out the result that the impact of writing is the same for all civilisations, however they may be developing. And it has to make historical phenomena—in particular, those of record-keeping—obey the same laws for different civilisations, however they may find their measures of memory and tradition affected by their literacy. And it has to make all such effects on development reciprocal. That is to say, if you are in a society and your literacy affects your estimate of knowledge outside the society, there must be an exactly similar change in the estimate which people outside the society make of knowledge inside it. input: This chapter is about something that Dr Whitehead handled with great cleverness. Dr Whitehead came up with the whole idea of a method that treats "points" as systems of events that have a finite size. When we support this method, we don't have to claim that mathematical points can't exist as simple things, or "particulars". We only have to claim that we have no good reason to think they do. What we know about points is that they are useful in a technical way, so useful that we need to find a meaning for the statements in which they appear as symbols. But there is no reason to deyn that a point has structure. In fact, there are two reasons to give a point structure. One is the well-known argument of Occam's razor: we can build structures that have the mathematical properties of points, and to assume that points exist in some other sense is a conclusion that is useless for science and not supported by any logical or scientific principle. The other argument is much harder to explain. But the more you study logical construction, the more you tend to value it. It is based on a rule that could be stated as a supplement to Occam's razor: "What is logically convenient is likely to be artificial." For us personally, the first example of this rlue was the definition of real numbers. Mathematicians found it convenient to assume that all series of rationals have limits, even though some don't have rational limits. So they assumed irrational limits, which they thought were of the same kind as rationals. Even though the method of Dedekind cuts was well known, nobody thought to say: An irrational is a Dedekind cut, or at least its lower part. But this definition solves all the problems. Now we have first ratios, which can't be irrational, then segments of the series of ratios. Segments that have a limit are rational, and segments that have no limit are irrational. The square root of 2 is the class of ratios whose square is less than 2. Segments of the series of ratios are real numbers. And the series of real numbers has both Dedekindian and Cantorian continuity. So it is mathematically convenient. But its logical structure is more complicated than that of the series of ratios. The logical analysis of mathematics gives many examples of this process, such as the construction of "ideal" points, lines, and planes mentioned in Chapter XX.

output: There is, in all these questions, a very great difficulty in avoiding confusion between what we can infer and what is in fact determined. Let us consider, for a moment, the various senses in which the future may be "determined." There is one sense—and a very important one—in which it is determined quite independently of scientific laws, namely, the sense that it will be what it will be. We all regard the past as determined simply by the fact that it has happened; but for the accident that memory works backward and not forward, we should regard the future as equally determined by the fact that it will happen. "But," we are told, "you cannot alter the past, while you can to some extent alter the future." This view seems to us to rest upon just those errors in regard to causation which it has been our object to remove. You cannot make the past other than it was—true, but this is a mere application of the law of contradiction. If you already know what the past was, obviously it is useless to wish it different. But also you cannot make the future other than it will be; this again is an application of the law of contradiction. And if you happen to know the future—e.g. in the case of a forthcoming eclipse—it is just as useless to wish it different as to wish the past different. "But," it will be rejoined, "our wishes can cause the future, sometimes, to be different from what it would be if they did not exist, and they can have no such effect upon the past." This, again, is a mere tautology. An effect being defined as something subsequent to its cause, obviously we can have no effect upon the past. But that does not mean that the past would not have been different if our present wishes had been different. Obviously, our present wishes are conditioned by the past, and therefore could not have been different unless the past had been different; therefore, if our present wishes were different, the past would be different. Of course, the past cannot be different from what it was, but no more can our present wishes be different from what they are; this again is merely the law of contradiction. The facts seem to be merely (1) that wishing generally depends upon ignorance, and is therefore commoner in regard to the future than in regard to the past; (2) that where a wish concerns the future, it and its realisation very often form a "practically independent system," i.e. many wishes regarding the future are realised. But there seems no doubt that the main difference in our feelings arises from the accidental fact that the past but not the future can be known by memory.

Consequently motion is something constructed in accordance with the laws of physics, or—it might be said—as a convenience in stating them; it cannot be one of the fundamental concepts of physics. Lastly, there is an argument which is difficult to state precisely, but which nevertheless has some weight. For Newton, motion was absolute, and a body in motion might be regarded as in a different state from a body at rest. But when motion was recognized as merely relative, laws of motion became laws as to relations to more or less distant bodies. They thus came to involve something like action at a distance—though this was disguised by the use of differential equations not always interpreted according to rigid Weierstrassian methods. If action at a distance is to be avoided, fundamental laws must be concerned with terms having finite spatio-temporal extension, and thus capable of contact and overlapping—in a word, with events rather than particles or impenetrable material units. This involves a re-interpretation of motion as it occurs in physics, which will be considered in a later chapter. For the present, concern is with the materials which will be required for this purpose as well as for the interpretation of other physical phenomena.

output: There is, in all these questions, a very great difficulty in avoiding confusion between what one can infer and what is in fact determined. Let one consider, for a moment, the various senses in which the future may be "determined." There is one sense—and a very important one—in which it is determined quite independently of scientific laws, namely, the sense that it will be what it will be. The past is regarded as determined simply by the fact that it has happened; but for the accident that memory works backward and not forward, the future would be regarded as equally determined by the fact that it will happen. "But," it is said, "the past cannot be altered, while the future can to some extent be altered." This view seems to rest upon just those errors in regard to causation which it has been the object to remove. The past cannot be made other than it was—true, but this is a mere application of the law of contradiction. If what the past was is already known, obviously it is useless to wish it different. But also the future cannot be made other than it will be; this again is an application of the law of contradiction. And if the future happens to be known—e.g. in the case of a forthcoming eclipse—it is just as useless to wish it different as to wish the past different. "But," it will be rejoined, "wishes can cause the future, sometimes, to be different from what it would be if they did not exist, and they can have no such effect upon the past." This, again, is a mere tautology. An effect being defined as something subsequent to its cause, obviously no effect can be had upon the past. But that does not mean that the past would not have been different if present wishes had been different. Obviously, present wishes are conditioned by the past, and therefore could not have been different unless the past had been different; therefore, if present wishes were different, the past would be different. Of course, the past cannot be different from what it was, but no more can present wishes be different from what they are; this again is merely the law of contradiction. The facts seem to be merely (1) that wishing generally depends upon ignorance, and is therefore commoner in regard to the future than in regard to the past; (2) that where a wish concerns the future, it and its realisation very often form a "practically independent system," i.e. many wishes regarding the future are realised. But there seems no doubt that the main difference in feelings arises from the accidental fact that the past but not the future can be known by memory.
